To roll back to the last commit, you have several options depending on what exactly you want to achieve:

## 1. Discard uncommitted changes and return to last commit state

Since you have modified `test_agent.py`, if you want to discard those changes and return to the last commit state:

```bash
git checkout -- test_agent.py
```

Or to discard all uncommitted changes:

```bash
git checkout -- .
```

Alternatively, you can use:

```bash
git restore test_agent.py
```

Or for all files:

```bash
git restore .
```

## 2. Reset to last commit (discarding all changes)

If you want to completely reset your working directory to match the last commit:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD
```

⚠️ **Warning**: This will permanently delete all uncommitted changes.

## 3. Undo the last commit but keep changes

If you want to undo the last commit but keep your changes in the working directory:

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1
```

## 4. Completely remove the last commit

If you want to completely remove the last commit and its changes:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD~1
```

⚠️ **Warning**: This permanently deletes the last commit and all its changes.

## Most likely what you want

Based on your git status showing modified files, you probably want option 1 or 2:

- **Option 1**: `git restore .` (safer, only affects uncommitted changes)
- **Option 2**: `git reset --hard HEAD` (more aggressive, same result in your case)

Both will take you back to the exact state of your last commit, discarding the changes to `test_agent.py`.

To go back to the specific commit `893ca1f7ec7579f68c801e5fec4e99fc33fb746b`, you have several options:

## 1. Reset your current branch to that commit (most common)

```bash
git reset --hard 893ca1f7ec7579f68c801e5fec4e99fc33fb746b
```

This will:
- Move your current branch pointer to that commit
- Reset your working directory to match that commit
- **Permanently delete** all commits after that point and uncommitted changes

## 2. Checkout that commit (temporary, read-only)

```bash
git checkout 893ca1f7ec7579f68c801e5fec4e99fc33fb746b
```

This will:
- Put you in a "detached HEAD" state
- Let you explore the code at that commit
- **Not affect** your branch or commit history
- To return to your current branch: `git checkout main`

## 3. Create a new branch from that commit

```bash
git checkout -b new-branch-name 893ca1f7ec7579f68c801e5fec4e99fc33fb746b
```

This will:
- Create a new branch starting from that commit
- Keep your original branch intact
- Switch to the new branch

## 4. Soft reset (keep changes in staging)

```bash
git reset --soft 893ca1f7ec7579f68c801e5fec4e99fc33fb746b
```

This will:
- Move your branch pointer to that commit
- Keep all changes from newer commits in your staging area
- Allow you to recommit or modify them

## Recommendation

If you want to **permanently** go back to that commit and discard everything after it, use **option 1**:

```bash
git reset --hard 893ca1f7ec7579f68c801e5fec4e99fc33fb746b
```

⚠️ **Warning**: This will permanently delete all commits and changes after `893ca1f`. Make sure this is what you want before proceeding.

If you're unsure, start with **option 2** to explore that commit safely first.

To sync your local repository with the main branch, you have a couple of options depending on what you want to achieve:

## 1. Push your reset state to remote main (force push)

If you want to make the remote main branch match your local state (the commit you reset to):

```bash
git push origin main --force
```

⚠️ **Warning**: This will overwrite the remote main branch and **permanently delete** all commits after `893ca1f` for everyone. Only do this if:
- You're the only one working on this repository, OR
- You have permission and everyone agrees to lose those commits

## 2. Pull latest changes from remote main

If you want to get the latest changes from the remote main branch (essentially undoing your reset):

```bash
git pull origin main
```

Or if you want to be more explicit:

```bash
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
```

## 3. Reset to match remote main exactly

If you want to completely reset your local main to match the remote main:

```bash
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main
```

## 4. Force pull (if there are conflicts)

If the pull fails due to conflicts, you can force your local to match remote:

```bash
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main
```

## Which option should you choose?

- **Option 1** (`git push --force`): Use if you want everyone to go back to commit `893ca1f`
- **Option 2-4** (`git pull` or `git reset --hard origin/main`): Use if you want to get back to the latest remote state

## Most likely scenario

If you reset to an older commit and now want to get back to the current state, use:

```bash
git pull origin main
```

This will bring your local main branch back to sync with the remote main branch.
